claims.text: Adding approximately 5 atomic percent terbium to a refractory high-entropy alloy enhances its superconducting behavior.
Terbium addition modifies the electronic density of states near the Fermi level.
The terbium-modified alloy retains a disordered, single-phase solid solution.
The starting material is a terbium-free refractory high-entropy-alloy solid solution.
The starting material has low or marginal superconductivity.
Arc melting can produce a uniform solid solution containing approximately 5 atomic percent terbium.
Identical thermal processing conditions are sufficient to ensure that both samples are single-phase disordered alloys.
Terbium induces local electronic-environment modifications within the disordered solid solution.
Localized terbium f-electron states alter the density of states at the Fermi level.
The density-of-states modification can enhance electron-pairing interactions.
Approximately 5 atomic percent terbium does not trigger detrimental phase separation.
Fine-tuning electron count can counterbalance magnetic pair breaking caused by terbium f electrons.
The terbium-doped alloy will have a higher superconducting transition temperature than the terbium-free baseline.
The terbium-doped alloy will have a higher superconducting volume fraction than the terbium-free baseline.
The proposed enhancement applies only while the alloy remains a single-phase solid solution.
Above a terbium-content threshold of approximately 5–10 atomic percent, secondary phases or magnetic scattering may dominate and suppress superconductivity.

The balance between electronic-structure tuning and terbium-induced magnetic pair breaking is not known, so the optimal terbium concentration and net change in transition temperature require experiment.

contradictions.description: The conditions require experiments to be performed below the known baseline transition temperature, whereas identifying and comparing transition temperatures by temperature-dependent resistivity and susceptibility requires a scan spanning both sides of each transition.

The boundary excludes samples that develop secondary phases, but the falsification rule treats the appearance of secondary phases as falsification. Secondary-phase formation would instead place the sample outside the stated domain of the hypothesis unless phase retention itself is explicitly part of the causal prediction.
